Lemma A.1.

Let g:𝒳→ℝg:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} be another fitness function satisfying f⁡(a)≥f⁡(a′)⇔g⁡(a)≥g⁡(a′)f(a)\geq f(a^{\prime})\iff g(a)\geq g(a^{\prime}) for all a,a′∈𝒳a,a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}. Then, the weights defined in Equation 3 satisfies wα​(a,f,r)=wα​(a,g,r)w_{\alpha}(a;f,r)=w_{\alpha}(a;g,r) for any a∈𝒳a\in\mathcal{X} and distribution r∈Δ⁡(𝒳)r\in\Delta(\mathcal{X}).

Proof.

Let 𝒞={C1,C2,…​Cm}\mathcal{C}=\left\{C_{1},C_{2},\dots C_{m}\right\} be the set of equivalence classes under ff (equivalently under gg), i.e. for each i=1,…,mi=1,\dots,m, if a,a′∈Cia,a^{\prime}\in C_{i} then f⁡(a)=f⁡(a′)f(a)=f(a^{\prime}) and g⁡(a)=g⁡(a′)g(a)=g(a^{\prime}). We order these classes from best to worst: if 1≤i<j≤m1\leq i<j\leq m, then f⁡(a)>f⁡(a′)f(a)>f(a^{\prime}) for a∈Cia\in C_{i} and a′∈Cja^{\prime}\in C_{j}. This ordering is the same under ff and gg. Therefore the cumulative mass, under rr, of the union of the top classes is the same whether we view them through ff or through gg.

Let C⋆C^{\star} denote the (unique) cutoff class: the class such that the total rr-mass of classes strictly above C⋆C^{\star} is <α<\alpha while the mass of classes at or above C⋆C^{\star} is ≥α\geq\alpha. Since the class ordering is the same for ff and gg, the cutoff class C⋆C^{\star} is the same for both fitness functions. Consequently, the strict-above set and tie-at-cutoff set are also the same:

{a:f⁡(a)>τα​(r,f)}={a:g⁡(a)>τα​(r,g)}\displaystyle\{a:f(a)>\tau_{\alpha}(r;f)\}=\{a:g(a)>\tau_{\alpha}(r;g)\}
{a:f⁡(a)=τα​(r,f)}={a:g⁡(a)=τα​(r,g)}.\displaystyle\{a:f(a)=\tau_{\alpha}(r;f)\}=\{a:g(a)=\tau_{\alpha}(r;g)\}.

For the cases with ties, γ\gamma is chosen to allocate exactly the remaining mass needed to reach α\alpha from the cutoff class C⋆C^{\star}; this depends only on r⁡(C⋆)r(C^{\star}) and the mass strictly above it, both of which are the same for ff and gg. Hence the resulting weights coincide for all aa. ∎

The dynamics in Equation 4 contains a discontinuous function in wt​(a)w_{t}(a) due to the hard quantile selection. For later discussion on convergence of the process, we will also consider a soft-quantile selection with the smoothly relaxed selection weight being given by

wαsoft​(a,f,r)=σβ​(f⁡(a)−ταsoft​(r,f))w_{\alpha}^{\mathrm{soft}}(a;f,r)=\sigma_{\beta}(f(a)-\tau_{\alpha}^{\mathrm{soft}}(r;f)) (5)

where σβ​(x):=1/(1+e−β​x)\sigma_{\beta}(x):=1/(1+e^{-\beta x}) is the sigmoid-function and the α\alpha-threshold value, ταsoft​(rt,f)\tau^{\mathrm{soft}}_{\alpha}(r_{t};f), is defined implicitly as the value that solves

∑aσβ​(f⁡(a)−ταsoft​(rt,f))​rt​(a)=α\sum_{a}\sigma_{\beta}(f(a)-\tau^{\mathrm{soft}}_{\alpha}(r_{t};f))r_{t}(a)=\alpha

Under this smooth relaxation, BPJ is instead modelled as the discrete dynamics

pt+1​(a)=1α​σβ​(f⁡(a)−ταsoft​(rt,f))​rt​(a).\displaystyle p_{t+1}(a)=\frac{1}{\alpha}\sigma_{\beta}(f(a)-\tau^{\mathrm{soft}}_{\alpha}(r_{t};f))r_{t}(a). (6)
Remark A.2.

Both Equation 4 and Equation 6 implements frequency-dependent selection resulting in non-linear dynamics. If the selection weight wt​(a)w_{t}(a) depends only on aa (frequency-independent selection), then the update equation for the dynamics amounts to applying a linear operator T​p=w⁡(a)​[(1−η)​(M​pt)​(a)+η​pt​(a)]Tp=w(a)\left[(1-\eta)(Mp_{t})(a)+\eta p_{t}(a)\right] and then applying the renormalisation term ZtZ_{t}. An alternative that we are not considering in present work is to have selection be given by a Boltzmann-weight wt​(a)=eβ​f​(a)w_{t}(a)=e^{\beta f(a)}. This will retain the elitist selection character (with large β\beta implementing stricter elitism) while preserving linearity (outside of renormalisation), which would result in easier analysis.

A.3 What drives progress?

We derive the following Price equation-style (Price, 1970) result showing that diversity in fitness of a population, in the form a covariance, allows the selection process to drive progress in mean fitness of a population.

Lemma A.3.

Let f:𝒳→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} be any fitness function. Let r∈Δ⁡(𝒳)r\in\Delta(\mathcal{X}) and let w:𝒳→[0,∞)w:\mathcal{X}\to[0,\infty) satisfy 0<𝔼r​[w]<∞0<\mathbb{E}_{r}[w]<\infty. Define p⁡(a):=r⁡(a)​w​(a)∑a′r⁡(a′)​w​(a′)p(a):=\frac{r(a)w(a)}{\sum_{a^{\prime}}r(a^{\prime})w(a^{\prime})}, then the mean fitness under pp satisfies

𝔼p​[f⁡(a)]−𝔼r​[f⁡(a)]=Covr​[f⁡(a),w⁡(a)]𝔼r​[w​(a)].\mathbb{E}_{p}[f(a)]-\mathbb{E}_{r}[f(a)]=\frac{\mathrm{Cov}_{r}\left[f(a),w(a)\right]}{\mathbb{E}_{r}[w(a)]}.

In particular, if 𝔼r​[w]=α\mathbb{E}_{r}[w]=\alpha (as in the normalisation of both hard and soft α\alpha-quantile selection), then the selection-only gain is

𝔼p​[f]−𝔼r​[f]=1α​Covr​[f,w].\mathbb{E}_{p}[f]-\mathbb{E}_{r}[f]=\frac{1}{\alpha}\mathrm{Cov}_{r}\left[f,w\right].
Proof.

We calculate

𝔼p​[f]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{p}[f] =∑a∈𝒳f⁡(a)​p​(a)\displaystyle=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{X}}f(a)p(a)
=∑a∈𝒳f⁡(a)​r⁡(a)​w​(a)𝔼r​[w]\displaystyle=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{X}}f(a)\frac{r(a)w(a)}{\mathbb{E}_{r}[w]}
=𝔼r​[f​w]𝔼r​[w].\displaystyle=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{r}[fw]}{\mathbb{E}_{r}[w]}.

Therefore,

𝔼p​[f]−𝔼r​[f]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{p}[f]-\mathbb{E}_{r}[f] =𝔼r​[f​w]𝔼r​[w]−𝔼r​[f]\displaystyle=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{r}[fw]}{\mathbb{E}_{r}[w]}-\mathbb{E}_{r}[f]
=𝔼r​[f​w]−𝔼r​[f]​𝔼r​[w]𝔼r​[w]\displaystyle=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{r}[fw]-\mathbb{E}_{r}[f]\mathbb{E}_{r}[w]}{\mathbb{E}_{r}[w]}
=Covr​[f,w]𝔼r​[w].\displaystyle=\frac{\mathrm{Cov}_{r}\left[f,w\right]}{\mathbb{E}_{r}[w]}.

∎

This shows that the effect of selection on the mean fitness of the population r⁡(a)r(a) (which is a mixture of parent and offspring in our case) is purely beneficial since 𝔼r​[w]>0\mathbb{E}_{r}[w]>0 and the covariance is non-negative, since for fixed rr wα​(a,f,r)w_{\alpha}(a;f,r) is non-decreasing in ff resulting in non-negative covariance with ff.

We note that, by Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, Covr​[f,w]≤𝕍r​[f]​𝕍r​[w]\mathrm{Cov}_{r}[f,w]\leq\sqrt{\mathbb{V}_{r}[f]\mathbb{V}_{r}[w]} which makes variance 𝕍r​[f]\mathbb{V}_{r}[f] in fitness on the post-mutation population a necessary condition for progress. For hard quantile truncation, assuming there is no ties (no aa with f⁡(a)=τα​(rt,f)=:τf(a)=\tau_{\alpha}(r_{t};f)=:\tau), the covariance is given by

Covrt​[f,wt]\displaystyle\mathrm{Cov}_{r_{t}}\left[f,w_{t}\right]
=\displaystyle= 𝔼rt​[f⋅wt]−𝔼rt​[f⁡(a)]​𝔼rt​[wt]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{r_{t}}[f\cdot w_{t}]-\mathbb{E}_{r_{t}}[f(a)]\mathbb{E}_{r_{t}}[w_{t}]
=\displaystyle= ∑a:f⁡(a)>τrt(a)f(a)−α∑art(a)f(a)\displaystyle\sum_{a:f(a)>\tau}r_{t}(a)f(a)-\alpha\sum_{a}r_{t}(a)f(a)
=\displaystyle= (1−α)∑a:f⁡(a)>τrt(a)f(a)−α∑a:f⁡(a)<τrt(a)f(a).\displaystyle(1-\alpha)\sum_{a:f(a)>\tau}r_{t}(a)f(a)-\alpha\sum_{a:f(a)<\tau}r_{t}(a)f(a).

Thus, in this case, selection-only progress is driven by the (weighted) difference between the mean fitness in the top α\alpha-quantile and bottom (1−α)(1-\alpha)-quantile.

The mean fitness change Δ​f¯​(t):=𝔼pt+1​[f]−𝔼pt​[f]\Delta\bar{f}(t):=\mathbb{E}_{p_{t+1}}[f]-\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}}[f], between evolutionary steps is a combination of the above selection-only effect and the effect of mutation.

Proposition A.4.

Let f:𝒳→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} and suppose 0<Zt<∞0<Z_{t}<\infty. Then

Δ​f¯​(t)=\displaystyle\Delta\bar{f}(t)= (𝔼rt​[f]−𝔼pt​[f])⏟mutation term+(𝔼pt+1​[f]−𝔼rt​[f])⏟selection term\displaystyle\underbrace{\big(\mathbb{E}_{r_{t}}[f]-\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}}[f]\big)}_{\text{mutation term}}+\underbrace{\big(\mathbb{E}_{p_{t+1}}[f]-\mathbb{E}_{r_{t}}[f]\big)}_{\text{selection term}}
=\displaystyle= (1−η)​(𝔼M​pt​[f]−𝔼pt​[f])+Covrt​(f,wt)𝔼rt​[wt].\displaystyle(1-\eta)\left(\mathbb{E}_{Mp_{t}}[f]-\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}}[f]\right)+\frac{\mathrm{Cov}_{r_{t}}(f,w_{t})}{\mathbb{E}_{r_{t}}[w_{t}]}. (7)
Proof.

First, by linearity of expectation and the definition of rtr_{t},

𝔼rt​[f]=(1−η)​𝔼M​pt​[f]+η​𝔼pt​[f]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{r_{t}}[f]=(1-\eta)\mathbb{E}_{Mp_{t}}[f]+\eta\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}}[f]
⟹\displaystyle\implies 𝔼rt​[f]−𝔼pt​[f]=(1−η)​(𝔼M​pt​[f]−𝔼pt​[f]).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{r_{t}}[f]-\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}}[f]=(1-\eta)\left(\mathbb{E}_{Mp_{t}}[f]-\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}}[f]\right).

We then get the desired conclusion by applying Lemma A.3. ∎

In particular, if Zt=𝔼rt​[wt]=αZ_{t}=\mathbb{E}_{r_{t}}[w_{t}]=\alpha then

Δ​f¯​(t)=(1−η)​(𝔼M​pt​[f]−𝔼pt​[f])+1α​Covrt​(f,wt).\Delta\bar{f}(t)=(1-\eta)\Big(\mathbb{E}_{Mp_{t}}[f]-\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}}[f]\Big)+\frac{1}{\alpha}\mathrm{Cov}_{r_{t}}(f,w_{t}). (8)

So, improvements in mean fitness is a sum of two effects:

  • •

    the always beneficial (or at least non-deleterious) effect of selection driven by diversity in the population and

  • •

    whether the net effect of mutation is beneficial or deleterious.

Why is direct optimisation on f0​(a)=𝒞​(a​x)f_{0}(a)=\mathcal{C}(ax) hard?

We observe in the Figure 5 that directly optimising for the base (binary fitness function f0​(a)=𝒞⁡(a​x)∈{0,1}f_{0}(a)=\mathcal{C}(ax)\in\left\{0,1\right\} results in extremely slow progress and in fact does not converge to a solution within our budget. Under the base binary objective, the space of candidate attacks 𝒳\mathcal{X} splits into two sets A0={a:𝒞⁡(a​x)=0}A^{0}=\left\{a:\mathcal{C}(ax)=0\right\} and A1={a:𝒞⁡(a​x)=1}A^{1}=\left\{a:\mathcal{C}(ax)=1\right\}. We expect A1A^{1} to be an extremely sparse subset of 𝒳\mathcal{X} thus any reasonable initial distribution p0​(a)p_{0}(a) has mass p0​(A1)≪1p_{0}(A^{1})\ll 1. In practice, a given initial population of candidates A0A_{0} is unlikely to intersect A1A^{1} resulting in a mass of zero on A1A^{1} for the initial (empirical) distribution.

When mutation is local and small (as is the case in BPJ), then rt​(A1)≈pt​(A1)r_{t}(A^{1})\approx p_{t}(A^{1}). Consider the α\alpha-quantile selection, if pt​(A1)<αp_{t}(A^{1})<\alpha then the α\alpha-quantile threshold satisfies τα​(rt,f0)=0\tau_{\alpha}(r_{t};f_{0})=0. This means that all candidates in A1A^{1} get selection weight wt=1w_{t}=1, while those in A0A^{0} lie exactly at the cutoff and receive the tie weight γt\gamma_{t}. A direct calculation then gives 𝔼rt​[wt]=α\mathbb{E}_{r_{t}}[w_{t}]=\alpha and Covrt​(f0,wt)=pt​(A1)​(1−α)\mathrm{Cov}_{r_{t}}(f_{0},w_{t})=p_{t}(A^{1})(1-\alpha). From Lemma A.3, the effect of selection on mean fitness is given by

1α​Covrt​(f0,wt)=1−αα​pt​(A1)\frac{1}{\alpha}\mathrm{Cov}_{r_{t}}(f_{0},w_{t})=\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}p_{t}(A^{1})

which is a quantity that stays tiny for most tt. Without selection driven improvement, the effect of the evolutionary update reduce to a random walk in Δ⁡(𝒳)\Delta(\mathcal{X}) induced by the Markov kernel MM. If mutation acts locally (offspring are likely to be close to parent in some metric) and if A1A^{1} is sparse and disconnected, selection is unlikely to find purchase for many generations.

A.4 Lifting via continuation method

The solution employed by BPJ to overcome this intrinsic hardness is to consider curriculum learning or the continuation method. At a high-level, the aim of a curriculum is to relax the binary objective into a family of objectives that quantify the quality of approximate solutions, thus creating signal for evolutionary optimisation to act upon.

Formally, we introduce a continuous parameter q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1] controlling the noise level of the noisy input samples x′∼Nq,xx^{\prime}\sim N_{q,x}. The relaxed fitness function fq​(a)=𝔼x′∼Nq,x​[𝒞⁡(a​x′)]f_{q}(a)=\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}\sim N_{q,x}}\left[\mathcal{C}(ax^{\prime})\right] is then valued in a continuous space, [0,1][0,1]. We assume that fq​(a)f_{q}(a) is a smooth function in qq. Indeed, for fixed aa, fq​(a)f_{q}(a) is a polynomial in qq if the noisy sample Nq,xN_{q,x} is given by random independent token-level substitution.

The results in the previous section on discrete dynamical system transfer straightforwardly by setting the fitness function to be fqf_{q}. Writing the update operator for each q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1] as

Φq:Δ⁡(𝒳)\displaystyle\Phi_{q}:\Delta(\mathcal{X}) →Δ⁡(𝒳)\displaystyle\to\Delta(\mathcal{X})
p\displaystyle p ↦Sq​(R​(p))\displaystyle\mapsto S_{q}(R(p))

where RR is the mutation operator p↦r=(1−η)​M​p+η​pp\mapsto r=(1-\eta)Mp+\eta p that remain unchanged and SqS_{q} is the selection operator r↦1α​r​(a)​wα​(a,fq,r)r\mapsto\frac{1}{\alpha}r(a)w_{\alpha}(a;f_{q},r) implementing the α\alpha-quantile selection. Note that wαw_{\alpha} is defined in Equation 3. More explicitly,

pt+1q​(a)=1α​wα​(a,fq,rtq)​rtq​(a)\displaystyle p^{q}_{t+1}(a)=\frac{1}{\alpha}w_{\alpha}(a;f_{q},r^{q}_{t})r^{q}_{t}(a) (9)

Similarly, the progress in mean fitness over generations again depends on mutation load and Price-style selection effect term

Δ​f¯q​(t):=\displaystyle\Delta\bar{f}_{q}(t):= 𝔼pt+1q​[fq]−𝔼ptq​[fq]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{p^{q}_{t+1}}[f_{q}]-\mathbb{E}_{p^{q}_{t}}[f_{q}] (10)
=\displaystyle= (1−η)​(EM​ptq​[fq]−𝔼ptq​[fq])\displaystyle(1-\eta)\left(E_{Mp^{q}_{t}}[f_{q}]-\mathbb{E}_{p^{q}_{t}}[f_{q}]\right) (11)
+1α​Covrtq​[fq​(a),wα​(a,fq,rtq)].\displaystyle+\frac{1}{\alpha}\mathrm{Cov}_{r^{q}_{t}}[f_{q}(a),w_{\alpha}(a;f_{q},r^{q}_{t})]. (12)

Assuming that the classifier 𝒞\mathcal{C} allows noisy input to pass, we can reasonably assume that, as qq increases to 1, it becomes increasingly likely to get both noisy input sample x′∼Nq,xx^{\prime}\sim N_{q,x} and a​x′ax^{\prime} pass the monitor for most prefix aa1111 11 The prefix aa itself needs to be a non-harmful string or setting a=xa=x itself should also cause the monitor to flag a​x′ax^{\prime} since we do expect prefix-first processing of the input string.. That is to say, we expect that q↦fq​(a)q\mapsto f_{q}(a) and q↦𝔼a∼p0​[fq​(a)]q\mapsto\mathbb{E}_{a\sim p_{0}}\left[f_{q}(a)\right] to be monotonically increasing functions of qq for generic aa and initialisation distribution p0​(a)p_{0}(a).

However, progress in evolutionary dynamics Equation 9 is driven by fitness variance. We expect that the variance to be ≈0\approx 0 near both ends where q=0q=0 (too hard, as argued before) and q=1q=1 (too easy, since most random aa will pass). But, given a reasonable initialisation distribution p0p_{0} (e.g. uniform over 𝒳\mathcal{X} or broadly supported), we expect both 𝕍p0​[fq]\mathbb{V}_{p_{0}}[f_{q}] and Covp0​[fq​(a),wα​(a,fq,r0)]\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{0}}[f_{q}(a),w_{\alpha}(a;f_{q},r_{0})] to be positive and large for some q0q_{0}, thus making progress possible for that noise level.

Lemma A.5.

Let p0∈Δ⁡(𝒳)p_{0}\in\Delta(\mathcal{X}) and a∼p0a\sim p_{0}. Define mean and variance as functions of qq to be m⁡(q):=𝔼a∼p0​[fq​(a)]m(q):=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim p_{0}}[f_{q}(a)] and v⁡(q):=𝕍a∼p0​[fq​(a)]v(q):=\mathbb{V}_{a\sim p_{0}}[f_{q}(a)]. Assume

  1. 1.

    fqf_{q} is such that for every a∈𝒳a\in\mathcal{X}, the map q↦fq​(a)q\mapsto f_{q}(a) is real analytic on an open interval containing [0,1][0,1]. (e.g. with Nq,xN_{q,x} constructed by having each tokens in xx subjected to independent qq-probability of being replaced by random token).

  2. 2.

    there exist ϵ∈(0,1/2)\epsilon\in(0,1/2) such that the mean satisfies m⁡(0)≤ϵm(0)\leq\epsilon and m⁡(1)≥1−ϵm(1)\geq 1-\epsilon.

  3. 3.

    there exist a,a′∈supp⁡(p0)a,a^{\prime}\in\mathrm{supp}(p_{0}) such that fq​(a)≠fq​(a′)f_{q}(a)\neq f_{q}(a^{\prime}) for some q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1].

then there exist q0∈(0,1)q_{0}\in(0,1) such that m⁡(q0)∈(ϵ,1−ϵ)m(q_{0})\in(\epsilon,1-\epsilon) and the variance v⁡(q0)>0v(q_{0})>0.

Proof.

By continuity of m⁡(q)m(q) and the intermediate value theorem, there exist q∗∈[0,1]q^{*}\in[0,1] such that m⁡(q∗)=1/2m(q^{*})=1/2 and thus exist a open interval I⊂[0,1]I\subset[0,1] such that m⁡(I)⊂(ϵ,1−ϵ)m(I)\subset(\epsilon,1-\epsilon). Since 𝒳\mathcal{X} is finite, v⁡(q)v(q) is a finite sums and products of analytic functions and hence is itself analytic. Suppose for contradiction that v⁡(q)=0v(q)=0 for all q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1]. Then for all qq, the random variable fq​(a)f_{q}(a) is almost surely constant under p0p_{0}, i.e. fq​(a)=fq​(a′)f_{q}(a)=f_{q}(a^{\prime}) for all a,a′∈supp⁡(p0)a,a^{\prime}\in\mathrm{supp}(p_{0}) and all qq which contradicts our assumption. Thus, v⁡(q)>0v(q)>0 for some qq. Since v⁡(q)v(q) is not identically zero, by analyticity, the set of zeros of v⁡(q)v(q) contains no accumulation point and thus v⁡(q)v(q) is not identically zero on any open interval, including II. So there exist q0∈Iq_{0}\in I such that v⁡(q0)>0v(q_{0})>0. ∎

A.4.1 Within-level Convergence

In this section, we discuss convergence of the discrete dynamics in Equation 9 within a fixed noise level q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1]. Due to the machinery we require in this section and to avoid piece-wise smooth book keeping, we will analyse instead the version of the dynamics with smoothed or soft quantile selection as discussed in Equation 6, i.e. we consider

Φqsoft:p↦Sqsoft​(R⁡(p))\Phi^{\mathrm{soft}}_{q}:p\mapsto S^{\mathrm{soft}}_{q}(R(p))

where Sqsoft​(r)S^{\mathrm{soft}}_{q}(r) is the soft selection operator r↦1α​r​(a)​σβ​(fq​(a)−ταsoft​(r,fq))r\mapsto\frac{1}{\alpha}r(a)\sigma_{\beta}\left(f_{q}(a)-\tau^{\mathrm{soft}}_{\alpha}(r;f_{q})\right) implementing the soft α\alpha-quantile selection. Note that soft quantile selection approximates hard quantile selection in the β→∞\beta\to\infty limit. We will show that under fairly general conditions, fixed points exist. Then we provide sufficient conditions so that the ptp_{t} iterations converges to fixed points.

To start, we will show that this Φqsoft\Phi^{\mathrm{soft}}_{q} is well defined and has differentiable dependence on its input pp. We note that the mutation operator is a fixed linear operator on p∈Δ⁡(𝒳)p\in\Delta(\mathcal{X}) and it is thus smooth. For the selection operator SqS_{q}, it is a composition of smooth functions with an implicitly defined quantity, ταsoft\tau^{\mathrm{soft}}_{\alpha}. Thus it remains to show that ταsoft\tau^{\mathrm{soft}}_{\alpha} is well defined and is regular with respect to qq and rr.

Lemma A.6.

Fix α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) and β>0\beta>0. For any function f:𝒳→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} on the finite space 𝒳\mathcal{X} and any r∈Δ⁡(𝒳)r\in\Delta(\mathcal{X}), there exists a unique value ταsoft​(r,f)∈ℝ\tau^{\mathrm{soft}}_{\alpha}(r;f)\in\mathbb{R} satisfying

∑a∈𝒳r⁡(a)​σβ​(f⁡(a)−ταsoft​(r,f))=α.\sum_{a\in\mathcal{X}}r(a)\,\sigma_{\beta}\left(f(a)-\tau^{\mathrm{soft}}_{\alpha}(r;f)\right)=\alpha. (13)

Moreover, the map r↦ταsoft​(r,f)r\mapsto\tau^{\mathrm{soft}}_{\alpha}(r;f) is C1C^{1} on the interior of all faces of the simplex

Δ∘​(𝒳′):={r∈Δ⁡(𝒳′):r⁡(a)>0​∀a∈𝒳′}\Delta^{\circ}(\mathcal{X}^{\prime}):=\{r\in\Delta(\mathcal{X}^{\prime}):r(a)>0\ \forall a\in\mathcal{X}^{\prime}\}

for any 𝒳′⊂𝒳\mathcal{X}^{\prime}\subset\mathcal{X} and is continuous on all of Δ⁡(𝒳)\Delta(\mathcal{X}). If additionally q↦fq​(a)q\mapsto f_{q}(a) is C1C^{1} for every a∈𝒳a\in\mathcal{X}, then (r,q)↦ταsoft​(r,fq)(r,q)\mapsto\tau^{\mathrm{soft}}_{\alpha}(r;f_{q}) is C1C^{1} on Δ∘​(𝒳′)×[0,1]\Delta^{\circ}(\mathcal{X}^{\prime})\times[0,1] (and jointly continuous on Δ⁡(𝒳)×[0,1]\Delta(\mathcal{X})\times[0,1]). In this case, writing τ⁡(r,q):=ταsoft​(r,fq)\tau(r,q):=\tau^{\mathrm{soft}}_{\alpha}(r;f_{q}), their derivatives with respect to r⁡(a)r(a) for a∈𝒳′a\in\mathcal{X}^{\prime} are given by

∂τ∂r⁡(a)​(r,q)\displaystyle\frac{\partial\tau}{\partial r(a)}(r,q) =σβ​(fq​(a)−τ⁡(r,q))∑u∈𝒳r⁡(u)​σβ′​(fq​(u)−τ⁡(r,q)),\displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{\beta}\left(f_{q}(a)-\tau(r,q)\right)}{\sum_{u\in\mathcal{X}}r(u)\sigma_{\beta}^{\prime}\left(f_{q}(u)-\tau(r,q)\right)}, (14)
∂τ∂q​(r,q)\displaystyle\frac{\partial\tau}{\partial q}(r,q) =∑a∈𝒳r⁡(a)​σβ′​(fq​(a)−τ⁡(r,q))​∂qfq​(a)∑u∈𝒳r⁡(u)​σβ′​(fq​(u)−τ⁡(r,q)).\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{a\in\mathcal{X}}r(a)\sigma_{\beta}^{\prime}\left(f_{q}(a)-\tau(r,q)\right)\partial_{q}f_{q}(a)}{\sum_{u\in\mathcal{X}}r(u)\,\sigma_{\beta}^{\prime}\left(f_{q}(u)-\tau(r,q)\right)}. (15)
Proof.

Fix r∈Δ⁡(𝒳)r\in\Delta(\mathcal{X}) and define

Hr​(τ):=∑a∈𝒳r⁡(a)​σβ​(f⁡(a)−τ).H_{r}(\tau):=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{X}}r(a)\,\sigma_{\beta}\!\big(f(a)-\tau\big).

Since 𝒳\mathcal{X} is finite and σβ\sigma_{\beta} is continuous, HrH_{r} is continuous. Moreover,

limτ→−∞Hr​(τ)=∑ar⁡(a)⋅1=1\displaystyle\lim_{\tau\to-\infty}H_{r}(\tau)=\sum_{a}r(a)\cdot 1=1
limτ→+∞Hr​(τ)=∑ar⁡(a)⋅0=0.\displaystyle\lim_{\tau\to+\infty}H_{r}(\tau)=\sum_{a}r(a)\cdot 0=0.

Also HrH_{r} is strictly decreasing because for all τ∈ℝ\tau\in\mathbb{R},

dd​τHr(τ)=−∑a∈𝒳r(a)σβ′(f(a)−τ)<0,\frac{d}{d\tau}H_{r}(\tau)=-\sum_{a\in\mathcal{X}}r(a)\,\sigma_{\beta}^{\prime}\!\big(f(a)-\tau\big)<0,

where σβ′​(x)=β​σβ​(x)​(1−σβ​(x))>0\sigma_{\beta}^{\prime}(x)=\beta\sigma_{\beta}(x)(1-\sigma_{\beta}(x))>0 and ∑ar⁡(a)=1\sum_{a}r(a)=1. By the intermediate value theorem, there exists a (unique) τ\tau such that Hr​(τ)=αH_{r}(\tau)=\alpha. This defines ταsoft​(r,f)\tau^{\mathrm{soft}}_{\alpha}(r;f) uniquely. To prove regularity, define the function

G⁡(r,τ):=∑a∈𝒳r⁡(a)​σβ​(f⁡(a)−τ)−α,G(r,\tau):=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{X}}r(a)\,\sigma_{\beta}\!\big(f(a)-\tau\big)-\alpha,

so that ταsoft​(r,f)\tau^{\mathrm{soft}}_{\alpha}(r;f) is characterised by G⁡(r,τ)=0G(r,\tau)=0. We have

∂τG(r,τ)=−∑a∈𝒳r(a)σβ′(f(a)−τ).\partial_{\tau}G(r,\tau)=-\sum_{a\in\mathcal{X}}r(a)\,\sigma_{\beta}^{\prime}\!\big(f(a)-\tau\big).

Fix arbitrary 𝒳′⊂𝒳\mathcal{X}^{\prime}\subset\mathcal{X}. If r∈Δ∘​(𝒳′)r\in\Delta^{\circ}(\mathcal{X}^{\prime}), meaning r⁡(a)>0r(a)>0 for all a∈𝒳′a\in\mathcal{X}^{\prime}, then ∂τG⁡(r,τ)<0\partial_{\tau}G(r,\tau)<0 for all τ\tau, in particular it is nonzero at the root. Therefore, by the implicit function theorem applied near rr as an element of Δ∘​(𝒳′)\Delta^{\circ}(\mathcal{X}^{\prime}), the map r↦ταsoft​(r,f)r\mapsto\tau^{\mathrm{soft}}_{\alpha}(r;f) is C1C^{1} on Δ∘​(𝒳′)\Delta^{\circ}(\mathcal{X}^{\prime}), and differentiation of G⁡(r,τ⁡(r))≡0G(r,\tau(r))\equiv 0 yields (14). Continuity on the whole simplex Δ⁡(𝒳)\Delta(\mathcal{X}) follows because the root of G⁡(r,τ)G(r,\tau) is unique for every r∈Δ⁡(𝒳)r\in\Delta(\mathcal{X}) as shown above and and Hr​(τ)H_{r}(\tau) depends continuously on (r,τ)(r,\tau) in the finite setting.

Finally, assume q↦fq​(a)q\mapsto f_{q}(a) is C1C^{1} for every aa. Consider

G~​(r,q,τ):=∑a∈𝒳r⁡(a)​σβ​(fq​(a)−τ)−α.\tilde{G}(r,q,\tau):=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{X}}r(a)\,\sigma_{\beta}\!\big(f_{q}(a)-\tau\big)-\alpha.

For r∈Δ∘​(𝒳′)r\in\Delta^{\circ}(\mathcal{X}^{\prime}), we have

∂τG~(r,q,τ)=−∑ar(a)σβ′(fq(a)−τ)≠0,\partial_{\tau}\tilde{G}(r,q,\tau)=-\sum_{a}r(a)\,\sigma_{\beta}^{\prime}\!\big(f_{q}(a)-\tau\big)\neq 0,

so the implicit function theorem implies (r,q)↦ταsoft​(r,fq)(r,q)\mapsto\tau^{\mathrm{soft}}_{\alpha}(r;f_{q}) is C1C^{1} on Δ∘​(𝒳′)×[0,1]\Delta^{\circ}(\mathcal{X}^{\prime})\times[0,1]. Differentiating G~​(r,q,τ⁡(r,q))≡0\tilde{G}(r,q,\tau(r,q))\equiv 0 with respect to qq yields (15). Joint continuity on Δ⁡(𝒳)×[0,1]\Delta(\mathcal{X})\times[0,1] follows as above. ∎

The results above show that Φqsoft\Phi^{\mathrm{soft}}_{q} is a continuous endomorphism on the convex space of simplex Δ⁡(𝒳)\Delta(\mathcal{X}) and is C1C^{1} on the interior Δ∘​(𝒳)\Delta^{\circ}(\mathcal{X}) (more generally, on the relative interior of each face). Therefore, by Brouwer’s fixed point theorem, we get existence of fixed point.

Theorem A.7.

For all qq, there exist a distribution p∈Δ⁡(𝒳)p\in\Delta(\mathcal{X}) satisfying the fixed point equation p=Φqsoft​(p)p=\Phi^{\mathrm{soft}}_{q}(p).

We denote such equilibrium or fixed point distribution at noise level qq as pq⋆∈Δ⁡(𝒳)p^{\star}_{q}\in\Delta(\mathcal{X}). This shows existence. We will now move to discuss conditions for convergence.

Remark A.8 (Why global contraction is unlikely).

A sufficient condition for global convergence of the dynamics pt+1=Φqsoft​(pt)p_{t+1}=\Phi^{\mathrm{soft}}_{q}(p_{t}) would be for Φqsoft\Phi^{\mathrm{soft}}_{q} to be a contraction map on Δ⁡(𝒳)\Delta(\mathcal{X}) with a probability metric such as total variation. However, such condition is not expected to hold in BPJ under the current mutation operation that does not perform strong mixing over the entire search space of candidates. To explain why intuitively, we note that the elitist quantile selection is inherently sensitive: it renormalises mass onto the top-α\alpha region, so a small perturbation of the current population can shift the implicit cutoff ταsoft​(r,fq)\tau^{\mathrm{soft}}_{\alpha}(r;f_{q}) and reweight a nontrivial fraction of the population. This introduces an effective expansion factor on the order of 1/α1/\alpha: when α\alpha is small (strong elitism), selection tends to amplify differences between populations rather than shrink them. In other words, two slightly different parent distribution can becomes more different after selection. Local mutation does not compensate for this, since edit-based mutation mixes slowly in total variation. Consequently, any global Lipschitz bound is typically ≥1\geq 1 and thus vacuous.

Remark A.9 (Boundary/face issues).

For the soft update, σβ∈(0,1)\sigma_{\beta}\in(0,1) implies that selection does not create exact zeros: pt+1​(a)=0⇔rt​(a)=0p_{t+1}(a)=0\iff r_{t}(a)=0. Thus support changes arise only from the mutation operator RR. In this section we state local convergence conditions around interior equilibria pq⋆∈Δ∘​(𝒳)p^{\star}_{q}\in\Delta^{\circ}(\mathcal{X}), which avoids bookkeeping on simplex faces. If an equilibrium lies on the boundary (possible when MM has zero transition probabilities), the same local-stability argument applies on the invariant face containing the equilibrium by restricting derivatives to the face tangent space. For hard quantile selection, zeros can be created by truncation itself and face issues become substantially more prominent.

We turn our focus instead on local stability.

Proposition A.10 (Within-level local convergence near a stable interior equilibrium).

Let q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1] be fixed. Let pq⋆∈Δ∘​(𝒳)p^{\star}_{q}\in\Delta^{\circ}(\mathcal{X}) satisfy the fixed point equation pq⋆=Φqsoft​(pq⋆)p^{\star}_{q}=\Phi^{\mathrm{soft}}_{q}(p^{\star}_{q}). Since Φqsoft\Phi^{\mathrm{soft}}_{q} is C1C^{1} on Δ∘​(𝒳)\Delta^{\circ}(\mathcal{X}) (Lemma A.6), its Jacobian Dp​Φqsoft​(pq⋆)D_{p}\Phi^{\mathrm{soft}}_{q}(p^{\star}_{q}) is well-defined. Let

T:={u∈ℝ𝒳:∑a∈𝒳u⁡(a)=0}T:=\left\{u\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{X}}:\sum_{a\in\mathcal{X}}u(a)=0\right\}

be the tangent space of the simplex at interior points, and let

Jq:=Dp​Φqsoft​(pq⋆)|T:T→TJ_{q}:=D_{p}\Phi^{\mathrm{soft}}_{q}(p^{\star}_{q})\big|_{T}:T\to T

denote the Jacobian. If the spectral radius satisfies ρ⁡(Jq)<1\rho(J_{q})<1, then pq⋆p^{\star}_{q} is locally attracting: there exist ϵ>0\epsilon>0, κ∈(0,1)\kappa\in(0,1) and a norm ∥⋅∥⋆\|\cdot\|_{\star} on TT such that for all p0∈Bϵ​(pq⋆)∩Δ⁡(𝒳)p_{0}\in B_{\epsilon}(p^{\star}_{q})\cap\Delta(\mathcal{X}), the iterates pt+1=Φqsoft​(pt)p_{t+1}=\Phi^{\mathrm{soft}}_{q}(p_{t}) satisfy

‖pt−pq⋆‖⋆≤κt​‖p0−pq⋆‖⋆for all ​t≥0.\|p_{t}-p^{\star}_{q}\|_{\star}\leq\kappa^{t}\|p_{0}-p^{\star}_{q}\|_{\star}\qquad\text{for all }t\geq 0.

Equivalently, for any fixed norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| on TT there exist C≥1C\geq 1 and κ∈(0,1)\kappa\in(0,1) (possibly different) such that ‖pt−pq⋆‖≤C​κt​‖p0−pq⋆‖\|p_{t}-p^{\star}_{q}\|\leq C\kappa^{t}\|p_{0}-p^{\star}_{q}\|.

Proof sketch.

Because ρ⁡(Jq)<1\rho(J_{q})<1 on the finite-dimensional space TT, there exists a norm ∥⋅∥⋆\|\cdot\|_{\star} on TT such that the induced operator norm satisfies ‖Jq‖⋆<1\|J_{q}\|_{\star}<1. By continuity of D​ΦqsoftD\Phi^{\mathrm{soft}}_{q} on the interior, there exists a neighborhood U⊂Δ∘​(𝒳)U\subset\Delta^{\circ}(\mathcal{X}) of pq⋆p^{\star}_{q} on which supp∈U‖D​Φqsoft​(p)‖⋆≤κ<1\sup_{p\in U}\|D\Phi^{\mathrm{soft}}_{q}(p)\|_{\star}\leq\kappa<1. Therefore Φqsoft\Phi^{\mathrm{soft}}_{q} is a contraction on UU in the metric induced by ∥⋅∥⋆\|\cdot\|_{\star}, and Banach’s fixed-point theorem yields geometric convergence of iterates started in UU. ∎

Within a fixed qq, Proposition A.10 provides a sufficient condition for convergence (geometric rate) from a warm start that lies in the local attraction neighborhood of pq⋆p^{\star}_{q}. Continuation across levels requires that the equilibrium (or the final iterate) obtained at level qq lies inside the attraction neighborhood of an equilibrium at the next level q−Δ​qq-\Delta q. In the next section about continuation, we will turn our attention to conditions that ensures that these basin overlap holds along an equilibrium branch.

A.4.2 Continuation

We now aim to provide reasonable sufficient conditions that allow for continuation of a found fixed point pq⋆p^{\star}_{q} at level qq to lower noise-level q=q−δ​qq=q-\delta q and whether this can continue to q=0q=0. We will again focus on the interior Δ∘​(𝒳)\Delta^{\circ}(\mathcal{X}) to avoid technicalities with boundary and face of simplex book-keeping.

We now give an inverse function type result that show sufficient condition that we can locally track the equilibria across qq-levels.

Theorem A.11 (Local continuation of soft-quantile equilibria).

Fix α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), β>0\beta>0, and consider the soft-selection update map Φqsoft​(p):=Sqsoft​(R⁡(p))\Phi^{\mathrm{soft}}_{q}(p):=S^{\mathrm{soft}}_{q}(R(p)). Assume q↦fq​(a)q\mapsto f_{q}(a) is C1C^{1} for every a∈𝒳a\in\mathcal{X}. Let q0∈(0,1)q_{0}\in(0,1) and suppose p0∈Δ∘​(𝒳)p_{0}\in\Delta^{\circ}(\mathcal{X}) is a fixed point satisfying p0=Φq0soft​(p0)p_{0}=\Phi^{\mathrm{soft}}_{q_{0}}(p_{0}). Define the tangent space

T𝒳:={u∈ℝ𝒳:∑au⁡(a)=0}.T_{\mathcal{X}}:=\left\{u\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{X}}:\sum_{a}u(a)=0\right\}.

Assume that the linear map

(I−Dp​Φq0soft​(p0))|T𝒳:T𝒳→T𝒳(I-D_{p}\Phi^{\mathrm{soft}}_{q_{0}}(p_{0}))\big|_{T_{\mathcal{X}}}:T_{\mathcal{X}}\to T_{\mathcal{X}}

is invertible. Then there exists ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and a unique C1C^{1} curve q↦pq⋆∈Δ∘​(𝒳)q\mapsto p^{\star}_{q}\in\Delta^{\circ}(\mathcal{X}) defined for q∈(q0−ϵ,q0+ϵ)q\in(q_{0}-\epsilon,q_{0}+\epsilon) such that pq0⋆=p0p^{\star}_{q_{0}}=p_{0} and pq⋆=Φqsoft​(pq⋆)p^{\star}_{q}=\Phi^{\mathrm{soft}}_{q}(p^{\star}_{q}) for all such qq. If additionally the spectral radius of Dp​Φq0soft​(p0)D_{p}\Phi^{\mathrm{soft}}_{q_{0}}(p_{0}) restricted to T𝒳T_{\mathcal{X}} is strictly less than 11, then p0p_{0} is a locally attracting equilibrium for the iteration p←Φq0soft​(p)p\leftarrow\Phi^{\mathrm{soft}}_{q_{0}}(p), and the continued equilibria pq⋆p^{\star}_{q} remain locally attracting for all qq sufficiently close to q0q_{0}.

Proof sketch.

Define F⁡(p,q):=Φqsoft​(p)−pF(p,q):=\Phi^{\mathrm{soft}}_{q}(p)-p. Fixed points are exactly the zeros of FF. Lemma A.6 has shown that ταsoft​(r,fq)\tau_{\alpha}^{\mathrm{soft}}(r;f_{q}) is C1C^{1}, and thus (p,q)↦Φqsoft​(p)(p,q)\mapsto\Phi^{\mathrm{soft}}_{q}(p) is C1C^{1} in a neighborhood of (p0,q0)(p_{0},q_{0}) in Δ∘​(𝒳)×(q0−δ,q0+δ)\Delta^{\circ}(\mathcal{X})\times(q_{0}-\delta,q_{0}+\delta). Therefore FF is C1C^{1} there.

The derivative with respect to pp at (p0,q0)(p_{0},q_{0}) is Dp​F​(p0,q0)=Dp​Φq0soft​(p0)−ID_{p}F(p_{0},q_{0})=D_{p}\Phi^{\mathrm{soft}}_{q_{0}}(p_{0})-I. By assumption, Dp​F​(p0,q0)D_{p}F(p_{0},q_{0}) is invertible on the tangent space T𝒳T_{\mathcal{X}}.Applying the implicit function theorem in local coordinates existence and uniqueness of a C1C^{1} curve q↦pq⋆q\mapsto p^{\star}_{q} solving F⁡(pq⋆,q)=0F(p^{\star}_{q},q)=0 near q0q_{0}. Local attractivity follows from similar consideration in Proposition A.10. Finally, continuity of the Jacobian implies the same holds for qq in a neighborhood of q0q_{0}. ∎

Remark A.12 (Sensitivity and tracking fixed point).

Under the assumptions of Theorem A.11 above, the fixed-point family q↦pq⋆q\mapsto p_{q}^{\star} is C1C^{1} on (q0−ϵ,q0+ϵ)(q_{0}-\epsilon,q_{0}+\epsilon), and differentiating the fixed-point equation pq⋆=Φqsoft​(pq⋆)p_{q}^{\star}=\Phi_{q}^{\mathrm{soft}}(p_{q}^{\star}) yields the identity differential equation characterizing the continued fixed points

dd​q​pq⋆=(I−Dp​Φqsoft​(pq⋆))−1​∂qΦqsoft​(pq⋆).\frac{d}{dq}p_{q}^{\star}=\left(I-D_{p}\Phi_{q}^{\mathrm{soft}}(p_{q}^{\star})\right)^{-1}\partial_{q}\Phi_{q}^{\mathrm{soft}}(p_{q}^{\star}). (16)

Equation (16) is the standard continuation formula. And it also shows that continuation becomes ill-conditioned when I−Dp​ΦqsoftI-D_{p}\Phi_{q}^{\mathrm{soft}} is nearly singular (e.g. near a bifurcation). Near singularities, we get

  1. 1.

    Sensitivity to qq. dd​q​pq⋆\frac{d}{dq}p^{\star}_{q} becoming large implying small changes in qq moves equilibria very far.

  2. 2.

    Critical slowing down. Within level dynamics converge very slowly because contraction rate κ=≈1\kappa=\approx 1.

This relates to BPJ’s discrete continuation schedule. Suppose additionally that for qq in some interval the equilibrium pq⋆p_{q}^{\star} is uniformly locally attracting, i.e. there exist ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and κ∈(0,1)\kappa\in(0,1) such that for all such qq the map Φqsoft\Phi_{q}^{\mathrm{soft}} is κ\kappa-contractive on the ball Bϵ​(pq⋆)B_{\epsilon}(p_{q}^{\star}). Then, if BPJ reduces noise in steps q←q−Δ​qq\leftarrow q-\Delta q that are small enough that the previous equilibrium pq⋆p^{\star}_{q} lies inside the attraction neighborhood of the next equilibrium pq−Δ​q⋆p^{\star}_{q-\Delta q} (e.g. ‖pq⋆−pq−Δ​q⋆‖1<ϵ\|p^{\star}_{q}-p^{\star}_{q-\Delta q}\|_{1}<\epsilon), iterating p←Φq−Δ​qsoft​(p)p\leftarrow\Phi_{q-\Delta q}^{\mathrm{soft}}(p) for a few steps keeps the population within the basin and therefore tracks the moving equilibrium. Using (16), a sufficient informal condition is

Δ​q⋅sups∈[q−Δ​q,q]‖dd​s​ps⋆‖1≪ϵ,\Delta q\cdot\sup_{s\in[q-\Delta q,q]}\Bigl\|\frac{d}{ds}p_{s}^{\star}\Bigr\|_{1}\;\ll\;\epsilon,

i.e. the schedule step should be small compared with the local “speed” of the equilibrium. When I−Dp​Φqsoft​(pq⋆)I-D_{p}\Phi_{q}^{\mathrm{soft}}(p_{q}^{\star}) becomes nearly singular, the derivative dd​q​pq⋆\frac{d}{dq}p_{q}^{\star} can become large, indicating that smaller Δ​q\Delta q (or more within-level iterations) are required for stable continuation.

Note that in Figure 4 and Figure 9, we do see both successful continuation where noise-level rapidly decreases (little within level iteration needed) and also longer plateaus where within level improvements stalls.

A.4.3 Conditions for success: alignment between fqf_{q} and the base objective

Having convergence to a fixed point pq∗p^{*}_{q} for q=0q=0 is not sufficient to guarantee that discovered fixed point p0⋆p^{\star}_{0} is a good solution in the sense of having significant probability mass on the set of successful attacks. In this section, we will derive sufficient conditions for the continuation method to discover such good solutions for base objective. As before, these conditions split into within-level and across-level conditions We will provide sufficient conditions for

  1. 1.

    within-level: conditions needed for evolutionary updates according to fqf_{q} to also improves the base objective f0f_{0}.

  2. 2.

    across-level: conditions needed for equilibria tracking to further improve f0f_{0}.

Within level conditions.

Recall that the base objective function is f0​(a)=𝒞⁡(a​x)∈{0,1}f_{0}(a)=\mathcal{C}(ax)\in\left\{0,1\right\}. We will denote the set of successful attacks and its complement as

A1:={a∈𝒳:𝒞⁡(a​x)=1}A0:=𝒳∖A1.A^{1}:=\left\{a\in\mathcal{X}:\mathcal{C}(ax)=1\right\}\quad A^{0}:=\mathcal{X}\setminus A^{1}.

Let 1A1​(a)\mathrm{1}_{A^{1}}(a) denote the indicator function for A1A^{1}. At the tt-iteration within noise level qq, the state of the population is given by ptqp^{q}_{t}. We now examine how the base objective given by the mass on the success set A1A^{1} evolve under within-level evolutionary dynamics. Recall that the update equation is of the form

pt+1q​(a)=1α​wtq​(a)​rtq​(a)p^{q}_{t+1}(a)=\frac{1}{\alpha}w^{q}_{t}(a)r^{q}_{t}(a)

with the selection weight wtq​(a)w^{q}_{t}(a) differing depending on if we use hard or soft quantile selection. Define the base solution mass at ptqp^{q}_{t} as

πtq:=ptq​(A1)=Pra∼ptq⁡(a∈A1).\pi^{q}_{t}:=p^{q}_{t}(A^{1})=\Pr_{a\sim p^{q}_{t}}(a\in A^{1}). (17)

A direct specialization of Price-style identity in the same vein as Proposition A.4 shows that the within qq-level generational improvement Δ​πtq:=πt+1q−πtq\Delta\pi^{q}_{t}:=\pi^{q}_{t+1}-\pi^{q}_{t} is given by

Δ​πtq=\displaystyle\Delta\pi^{q}_{t}= (1−η)​[(M​ptq)​(A1)−πtq]⏟mutation effect on A1\displaystyle\underbrace{(1-\eta)\left[(Mp^{q}_{t})(A^{1})-\pi^{q}_{t}\right]}_{\text{mutation effect on $A^{1}$}} (18)
+1α​Covrtq​(1A1​(a),wtq​(a))⏟selection effect under fq.\displaystyle+\underbrace{\frac{1}{\alpha}\mathrm{Cov}_{r^{q}_{t}}(\mathrm{1}_{A^{1}}(a),w^{q}_{t}(a))}_{\text{selection effect under $f_{q}$}}. (19)

Using the fact that the indicator function 1A1\mathrm{1}_{A^{1}} is binary valued, direct calculation show that the covariance term can be expressed as

Covrtq​(1A1​(a),wtq​(a))=ρtq​(1−ρtq)​Γtq\mathrm{Cov}_{r^{q}_{t}}(\mathrm{1}_{A^{1}}(a),w^{q}_{t}(a))=\rho^{q}_{t}(1-\rho^{q}_{t})\Gamma^{q}_{t}

where ρtq:=rtq​(A1)\rho^{q}_{t}:=r^{q}_{t}(A^{1}) is the mass of the post-mutation mixture that is on A1A^{1} and Γtq\Gamma^{q}_{t} is the alignment factor defined by

Γtq\displaystyle\Gamma^{q}_{t} :=𝔼rtq​[wtq|A1]−𝔼rtq​[wtq|A0]\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{r^{q}_{t}}\left[w^{q}_{t}|A^{1}\right]-\mathbb{E}_{r^{q}_{t}}\left[w^{q}_{t}|A^{0}\right]
=1ρtq​∑a∈A1rtq​(a)​wtq​(a)−11−ρtq​∑a∈A0rtq​(a)​wtq​(a).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\rho^{q}_{t}}\sum_{a\in A^{1}}r^{q}_{t}(a)w^{q}_{t}(a)-\frac{1}{1-\rho^{q}_{t}}\sum_{a\in A^{0}}r^{q}_{t}(a)w^{q}_{t}(a).

Observe that, under hard quantile selection,

Γtq=Pra∼rtq⁡[fq​(a)>τα|A1]⏟True positive rate (TPR)−Pra∼rtq⁡[fq​(a)>τα|A0]⏟False positive rate (FPR).\Gamma^{q}_{t}=\underbrace{\Pr_{a\sim r^{q}_{t}}\left[f_{q}(a)>\tau_{\alpha}|A^{1}\right]}_{\text{True positive rate (TPR)}}-\underbrace{\Pr_{a\sim r^{q}_{t}}\left[f_{q}(a)>\tau_{\alpha}|A^{0}\right]}_{\text{False positive rate (FPR)}}. (20)

Interpreting the condition fq​(a)>τα​(rtq,fq)f_{q}(a)>\tau_{\alpha}(r^{q}_{t};f_{q}) as positive selection of aa according to fqf_{q}-ranking, then the above has the interpretation as the difference between true positive rate (TPR) and false positive rate (FPR) under the distribution rtqr^{q}_{t}. That is to say, if Γtq>0\Gamma^{q}_{t}>0, solutions (elements of A1A^{1}) are more likely than non-solutions (elements of A0A^{0}) to be selected by the in the top-α\alpha quantile criterion. That is precisely the condition for selection to increase base solution mass. Combining the above, the base solution mass drift at a fixed noise level qq is

Δ​πtq=(1−η)​((M​ptq)​(A1)−πtq)+ρtq​(1−ρtq)α​Γtq.\Delta\pi^{q}_{t}=(1-\eta)\left((Mp^{q}_{t})(A^{1})-\pi^{q}_{t}\right)+\frac{\rho^{q}_{t}(1-\rho^{q}_{t})}{\alpha}\,\Gamma^{q}_{t}. (21)

This makes explicit the two requirements for increasing base solution mass at fixed qq:

  1. 1.

    mutation should not destroy A1A^{1} mass too aggressively, and

  2. 2.

    selection induced by fqf_{q} should be positively aligned with A1A^{1} in the sense of having Γtq>0\Gamma^{q}_{t}>0.

For consistent or monotone improvement of πtq\pi^{q}_{t} within level qq, we would need the benefit for increasing A1A^{1}-mass due to selection at level qq to consistently dominate the effect of mutation.

Across level continuation: transporting base success mass along a tracked equilibrium branch.

Assume the soft dynamics admits a locally attracting interior equilibrium branch q↦pq⋆∈Δ∘​(𝒳)q\mapsto p_{q}^{\star}\in\Delta^{\circ}(\mathcal{X}) satisfying pq⋆=Φqsoft​(pq⋆)p_{q}^{\star}=\Phi_{q}^{\mathrm{soft}}(p_{q}^{\star}) and that BPJ tracks this branch as qq decreases according to Theorem A.11 and Remark A.12). π⋆​(q):=pq⋆​(A1)=∑a∈A1pq⋆​(a).\pi^{\star}(q):=p_{q}^{\star}(A^{1})=\sum_{a\in A^{1}}p_{q}^{\star}(a). (22)

dd​q​π⋆​(q)\displaystyle\frac{d}{dq}\pi^{\star}(q) (23)
=∑a∈A1dd​q​pq⋆​(a)\displaystyle=\sum_{a\in A^{1}}\frac{d}{dq}p_{q}^{\star}(a) (24)
=∑a∈A1[(I−Dp​Φqsoft​(pq⋆))−1​∂qΦqsoft​(pq⋆)]​(a).\displaystyle=\sum_{a\in A^{1}}\left[\left(I-D_{p}\Phi_{q}^{\mathrm{soft}}(p_{q}^{\star})\right)^{-1}\partial_{q}\Phi_{q}^{\mathrm{soft}}(p_{q}^{\star})\right](a). (25)

Under the no bifurcation condition, the total base solution mass at the end of continuation is therefore given by π⋆​(q0)+Δ​π∗\pi^{\star}(q_{0})+\Delta\pi^{*} where Δ​π⋆:=π⋆​(0)−π⋆​(q0)\Delta\pi^{\star}:=\pi^{\star}(0)-\pi^{\star}(q_{0}) is the cumulative net change over continuation given by

Δ​π⋆\displaystyle\Delta\pi^{\star} =∫q00dd​q​π⋆​(q)​𝑑q\displaystyle=\int_{q_{0}}^{0}\frac{d}{dq}\pi^{\star}(q)dq
=∑a∈A1∫q00[(I−Dp​Φqsoft​(pq⋆))−1​∂qΦqsoft​(pq⋆)]​(a)​𝑑q.\displaystyle=\sum_{a\in A^{1}}\int_{q_{0}}^{0}\left[\left(I-D_{p}\Phi_{q}^{\mathrm{soft}}(p_{q}^{\star})\right)^{-1}\partial_{q}\Phi_{q}^{\mathrm{soft}}(p_{q}^{\star})\right](a)dq.

This net change in solution mass can be negative over the course of continuation. To obtain non-trivial solution mass π⋆​(0)\pi^{\star}(0), sufficient conditions include

  1. 1.

    we already have sufficient initial solution mass π⋆​(q0)\pi^{\star}(q_{0}) and ‖Δ​π⋆‖\|\Delta\pi^{\star}\| is small.

  2. 2.

    the net change Δ​π∗\Delta\pi^{*} is positive, meaning continuation serves, on average, to amplify base solution mass.

Remark A.13.

We argue that BPJ construction of the curriculum intend to achieve amplification, i.e. positive Δ​π⋆\Delta\pi^{\star}. At high noise levels, the relaxed objective fq​(a)=𝔼x′∼Nq,x​[𝒞⁡(a​x′)]f_{q}(a)=\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}\sim N_{q,x}}[\mathcal{C}(ax^{\prime})] can admit many spurious high-fitness candidates that exploit artifacts of the noisy distribution but do not generalise to the noiseless input xx (so they actually lie in A0A^{0}). As qq decreases, these noise-dependent candidates tend to lose fitness, while candidates that are robust to the removal of noise (and hence more likely to belong to A1A^{1}) retain their relative ranking. In this regime, lowering qq acts as a filter that progressively removes non-robust solutions, shifting equilibrium mass from A0A^{0} toward A1A^{1}, which corresponds to Δ​π⋆>0\Delta\pi^{\star}>0.

A.5 Summary

From the perspective of continuation method as formulated in this section, BPJ succeeds, in the sense of achieving non-trivial mass on the set of solutions, A1A^{1}, when the following conditions hold.

  1. 1.

    Easy initialisation (a noise level with usable optimisation signal). There exists a starting noise level q0∈(0,1]q_{0}\in(0,1] such that the relaxed fitness fq0f_{q_{0}} is neither too hard (nearly binary with essentially all mass at 00) nor too easy (nearly constant with essentially all mass at 11). Concretely, under a broad initial distribution p0p_{0}, the post-mutation mixture r0q0r_{0}^{q_{0}} should exhibit nontrivial variance in fq0f_{q_{0}} so that quantile selection produces a non-negligible covariance term (Proposition A.4). This is the regime where within-level evolution can reliably concentrate mass onto higher-fitness candidates rather than behaving like a near-random walk. Lemma A.5 gives a broad conditions under which this is true.

  2. 2.

    Successful equilibrium tracking (no abrupt changes to equilibria with small enough step size in noise reduction, Δ​q\Delta q). For q∈[0,q0]q\in[0,q_{0}], the within-level soft dynamics admits a locally attracting equilibrium (stable fixed point) pq⋆p_{q}^{\star}, and these equilibria form a locally smooth branch in qq. A sufficient condition for this local trackability is the non-degeneracy or invertibility condition of Theorem A.11 and together with local stability (Proposition A.10). Operationally, BPJ’s schedule must decrease qq in steps Δ​q\Delta q that are small enough that the terminal population at level qq warm-starts inside the attraction basin at level q−Δ​qq-\Delta q. When it does, the equilibrium follows the tracking equation shown in Remark A.12.

  3. 3.

    Alignment of relaxed objective with base objective (selection according to relaxed objective prefers true solutions). At each level qq, selection induced by fqf_{q} should preferentially retain candidates that are also successful on the base task. In our notation, this requires positive alignment Γtq>0\Gamma_{t}^{q}>0 in Equation 21. Or equivalently, TPR is higher than FPR under the fqf_{q} induced top-α\alpha selection rule. This ensures that, at fixed qq, selection contributes positively to the mass on the true success set A1A^{1} rather than concentrating on spurious high-fqf_{q} artifacts.

  4. 4.

    Amplification along continuation (success mass does not decay as q↓0q\downarrow 0). Along the tracked equilibrium branch q↦pq⋆q\mapsto p_{q}^{\star}, the base success mass π⋆​(q)=pq⋆​(A1)\pi^{\star}(q)=p_{q}^{\star}(A^{1}) should be non-decreasing as noise is removed (informally, dd​q​π⋆​(q)≤0\frac{d}{dq}\pi^{\star}(q)\leq 0 when decreasing qq toward 00. Intuitively, continuation should progressively filter out candidates whose apparent fitness relies on noise, reallocating mass toward candidates that remain high-ranked as q→0q\to 0.

These conditions are mostly consistent with BPJ’s design. The noisy-input relaxation produces a fitness landscape with optimisation signal at intermediate qq for selection to act upon. The optimised population of candidates are then used to warm start the search at a reduced noise level qq. A gradual noise reduction schedule is designed for successful equilibrium tracking. More importantly, the relaxed objective is designed in away to provide a gradient towards the set of base solutions: decreasing noise favors candidates whose high fitness is robust to perturbation of xx rather than attack that exploit noisy artifacts.

We note that the above are merely sufficient conditions that can be violated in actual systems. Indeed, observe in Figure 4 and Figure 9 that, while there are mostly rapid decrement of noise-level showing successful continuation, there are also plateaus (long stretches of iterations where BPJ stays within the same noise level) indicating possible critical slow down due to singularities in the dynamical system or possibly even equilibrium branch switching. However, as shown in the same figure, the process can still recover from such encounters.

A.6 Surrogate Fitness Function and Boundary Points

Recall that our fitness function fq​(a)f_{q}(a) is itself an expectation over a distribution of noisy input strings Nq,xN_{q,x}, something we cannot tractably compute in practice. We can only compute an estimator of fqf_{q} using a finite number of samples X={xi′:i=1,…k}X=\left\{x^{\prime}_{i}:i=1,\dots k\right\}, where each xi′x^{\prime}_{i} are assumed to be sampled i.i.d. from some sampling distribution μq​(x′)\mu_{q}(x^{\prime}). Therefore, even in the infinite candidate population limit, we do not have deterministic evolutionary update on pt​(a)p_{t}(a), but instead we get a stochastic update

p^t+1q​(a)=1Z^t​rtq​(a)​w^t​(a)\hat{p}^{q}_{t+1}(a)=\frac{1}{\hat{Z}_{t}}r^{q}_{t}(a)\hat{w}_{t}(a)

where w^t​(a)=wα​(a,f^q,rtq)\hat{w}_{t}(a)=w_{\alpha}(a;\hat{f}_{q},r^{q}_{t}) is a weighting factor that depends on the estimator used for fqf_{q}. In this section, we will

  • •

    formulate the sample policy, μB​P\mu^{BP} used by BPJ.

  • •

    show that μB​P\mu^{BP} results in a fitness function gg that is different from fqf_{q}, but still, in expectation, induces the same evolutionary dynamics under hard quantile selection.

  • •

    explain the advantage of μB​P\mu^{BP} over i.i.d. sampling with Nq,xN_{q,x} in terms of the query complexity, i.e. the number of samples, hence query of the classifier needed to obtain information on evolutionary fitness signal.

A.6.1 BP Sampling Induces a Biased but Rank-preserving Surrogate Fitness Function

For any given finite set X,A⊂𝒳X,A\subset\mathcal{X} and distribution p∈Δ⁡(𝒳)p\in\Delta(\mathcal{X}), define

f^​(a,X)\displaystyle\hat{f}(a,X) :=1|X|​∑x′∈X𝒞⁡(a​x′)\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{|X|}\sum_{x^{\prime}\in X}\mathcal{C}(ax^{\prime})
s^​(x′,A)\displaystyle\hat{s}(x^{\prime},A) :=1|A|​∑a∈A𝒞⁡(a​x′)\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{|A|}\sum_{a\in A}\mathcal{C}(ax^{\prime})
s¯p​(x′)\displaystyle\bar{s}_{p}(x^{\prime}) :=𝔼a∼p​[𝒞⁡(a​x′)]\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim p}\left[\mathcal{C}(ax^{\prime})\right]

Note that all of f^\hat{f}, s^\hat{s} and s¯\bar{s} take values in [0,1][0,1]. We will also formally define a BPs as follow.

Definition A.14.

Given a set of candidates A⊂𝒳A\subset\mathcal{X} with 2≤|A|<∞2\leq|A|<\infty, a boundary point (BP) is a sequence b∈𝒳b\in\mathcal{X}, thought of as a noisy version of some harmful input xx, such that there exist a,a′∈Aa,a^{\prime}\in A with 𝒞⁡(a​b)=0\mathcal{C}(ab)=0 and 𝒞⁡(a′​b)=1\mathcal{C}(a^{\prime}b)=1. An equivalent characterisation is that bb is a BP relative to AA if and only if s^​(b,A)∈(0,1)\hat{s}(b,A)\in(0,1). We will also consider the infinite population limit characterisation of a BP. We say that b∈𝒳b\in\mathcal{X} is a BP relative to a distribution p⁡(a)p(a) if s¯p​(b)∈(0,1)\bar{s}_{p}(b)\in(0,1). We will use ℬ​𝒫​(A)\mathcal{BP}(A) and ℬ​𝒫​(p)\mathcal{BP}(p) to denote the set of all BPs relative to any given finite set AA and distribution pp respectively.

Now, the two options for μq\mu_{q} we are considering are:

  1. 1.

    Take the sampling policy to be given by μqi​i​d=Nq,x\mu^{iid}_{q}=N_{q,x}. If XX consist of samples from NqN_{q}, this results in f^q​(a,X)\hat{f}_{q}(a,X) being an unbiased estimator of fq​(a)f_{q}(a).

  2. 2.

    Take the sampling policy to be given by μA(x′)=1ZANq,x(x′)1[x′∈ℬ𝒫(A)]\mu_{A}(x^{\prime})=\frac{1}{Z_{A}}N_{q,x}(x^{\prime})\mathrm{1}\left[x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{BP}(A)\right] with A={aj:j=1,…,m}A=\left\{a_{j}:j=1,\dots,m\right\} being a given set of candidates and ZA=∑b∈ℬ​𝒫​(A)Nq,x​(b)Z_{A}=\sum_{b\in\mathcal{BP}(A)}N_{q,x}(b) is the mass of ℬ​𝒫​(A)\mathcal{BP}(A) under Nq,xN_{q,x}. Here μA\mu_{A} is simply the distribution of boundary points relative to AA characterised by the following sampling process: sample b∼Nq,xb\sim N_{q,x} with rejection until bb is a BP. For formal analysis, we will again consider the infinite population limit, getting μq,pB​P(x′)=1Zp1[s¯p(x′)∈(0,1)]Nq,x(x′)\mu^{BP}_{q,p}(x^{\prime})=\frac{1}{Z_{p}}\mathrm{1}\left[\bar{s}_{p}(x^{\prime})\in(0,1)\right]N_{q,x}(x^{\prime}) where pp is some distribution over attack candidates and Zp=∑b∈ℬ​𝒫​(p)Nq,x​(b)Z_{p}=\sum_{b\in\mathcal{BP}(p)}N_{q,x}(b).

Under μqi​i​d\mu^{iid}_{q} and the hard quantile selection process we recover the same evolutionary process Equation 9 with weight given by Equation 3. But under sampling policy μq,pB​P\mu^{BP}_{q,p}, we will instead have an estimator of fqf_{q} with mean

gq,p​(a)=𝔼b∼μq,pB​P​[𝒞⁡(a​b)].g_{q,p}(a)=\mathbb{E}_{b\sim\mu^{BP}_{q,p}}\left[\mathcal{C}(ab)\right].

Since gq,p​(a)≠fq​(a)g_{q,p}(a)\neq f_{q}(a) typically, this is a biased estimator. This will a priori result in a new different evolutionary dynamics

p~t+1q​(a)=1α​rtq​(a)​wtB​P​(a)\tilde{p}^{q}_{t+1}(a)=\frac{1}{\alpha}r^{q}_{t}(a)w^{BP}_{t}(a)

where the post-mutation population mixture rtq​(a)r^{q}_{t}(a) remain unchanged but the selection weighting changed to wtB​P​(a)=wα​(a,gq,p,rtq)w^{BP}_{t}(a)=w_{\alpha}(a;g_{q,p},r^{q}_{t}).

Lemma A.15.

Let p∈Δ⁡(𝒳)p\in\Delta(\mathcal{X}) be a distribution over candidates. Zp=∑b∈ℬ​𝒫​(p)Nq,x​(b)Z_{p}=\sum_{b\in\mathcal{BP}(p)}N_{q,x}(b) be the probability mass of ℬ​𝒫p\mathcal{BP}_{p} under Nq,xN_{q,x}. Assuming Zp>0Z_{p}>0, then, for any aa in the support of pp, we have fq​(a)=Zp​gq,p​(a)+Cpf_{q}(a)=Z_{p}g_{q,p}(a)+C_{p} where CpC_{p} is a constant that depends only on pp. Therefore, for fixed pp, gq,pg_{q,p} is an affine transform of fqf_{q} which, in particular preserves the rank of fqf_{q}: fq​(a)>fq​(a′)⇔gq,p​(a)>gq,p​(a′)f_{q}(a)>f_{q}(a^{\prime})\iff g_{q,p}(a)>g_{q,p}(a^{\prime}).

Proof.

Let a∈supp⁡(p)a\in\mathrm{supp}(p) be given, then

fq​(a)\displaystyle f_{q}(a) =∑x′∈ℬ​𝒫​(p)Nq,x​(x′)​𝒞​(a​x′)+∑x′∉ℬ​𝒫​(p)Nq,x​(x′)​𝒞​(a​x′)\displaystyle=\sum_{x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{BP}(p)}N_{q,x}(x^{\prime})\mathcal{C}(ax^{\prime})+\sum_{x^{\prime}\not\in\mathcal{BP}(p)}N_{q,x}(x^{\prime})\mathcal{C}(ax^{\prime})
=Zp⋅gq,p​(a)+∑x′∉ℬ​𝒫​(p)Nq,x​(x′)​𝒞​(a​x′)\displaystyle=Z_{p}\cdot g_{q,p}(a)+\sum_{x^{\prime}\not\in\mathcal{BP}(p)}N_{q,x}(x^{\prime})\mathcal{C}(ax^{\prime})

It remains to show that the second term above does not depend on aa. Indeed, if x′∉ℬ​𝒫​(p)x^{\prime}\not\in\mathcal{BP}(p), then by the definition of ℬ​𝒫​(p)\mathcal{BP}(p), s¯p​(x′)=𝔼u∼p​[𝒞⁡(u​x′)]∈{0,1}\bar{s}_{p}(x^{\prime})=\mathbb{E}_{u\sim p}\left[\mathcal{C}(ux^{\prime})\right]\in\{0,1\}. Now, if s¯p​(x′)=0\bar{s}_{p}(x^{\prime})=0 then 𝒞⁡(u​x′)=0\mathcal{C}(ux^{\prime})=0 for any u∼pu\sim p with probability 11. Similarly, if s¯p​(x′)=1\bar{s}_{p}(x^{\prime})=1 then 𝒞⁡(u​x′)=1\mathcal{C}(ux^{\prime})=1 for any u∼pu\sim p with probability 11. Thus, we conclude that 𝒞⁡(u​x′)\mathcal{C}(ux^{\prime}) is pp-almost surely a constant in {0,1}\left\{0,1\right\}. Since a∈supp⁡(p)a\in\mathrm{supp}(p), the value of 𝒞⁡(a​x′)\mathcal{C}(ax^{\prime}) is only dependent on pp and not on aa itself. Hence, it the second term is a constant CpC_{p} independent of aa. ∎

Together with lemma Lemma A.1, we get wα​(a,gq,p,rtq)=wα​(a,fq,rtq)w_{\alpha}(a;g_{q,p},r^{q}_{t})=w_{\alpha}(a;f_{q},r^{q}_{t}) which mean the surrogate fitness function preserves the original evolutionary dynamics under hard quantile selection.

Remark A.16.

The surrogate gq,pg_{q,p} is rank-preserving for fixed pp (equivalently, for a fixed candidate set AA in the finite-population setting). In BPJ, AA evolves but remain close in edit distance for some iterations. The maintenance step (remove solved BPs and replenish) ensures that BB is refreshed so that it remains a set of BPs relative to the current AA, preserving informativeness of the surrogate over time.

A.6.2 Advantage of BP over i.i.d. sampling

The result below shows that, for hard quantile selection relative to a candidate distribution pp, non-BPs do not change the selection weighting and thus do not change the evolutionary dynamics.

Proposition A.17.

Let p⁡(a)p(a) be a distribution over candidates attacks (e.g. rtr_{t}) and let X⊂𝒳X\subset\mathcal{X} be a finite set of string (e.g. drawn from Nq,xN_{q,x}) and let XB​P:=X∩ℬ​𝒫​(p)X_{BP}:=X\cap\mathcal{BP}(p) be the subset of XX containing only BPs relative to pp. Then, the selection weight wα​(a,f^​(⋅,X),p)w_{\alpha}(a;\hat{f}(\cdot,X),p) depends on XX only through XB​PX_{BP}, i.e. wα​(a,f^​(⋅,X),p)=wα​(a,f^​(⋅,XB​P),p)w_{\alpha}(a;\hat{f}(\cdot,X),p)=w_{\alpha}(a;\hat{f}(\cdot,X_{BP}),p) for all a∈supp⁡(p)a\in\mathrm{supp}(p). We take f^​(⋅,∅)≡0\hat{f}(\cdot,\emptyset)\equiv 0 by convention.

Therefore, for all a∈supp⁡(p)a\in\mathrm{supp}(p),

f^​(a,X)\displaystyle\hat{f}(a,X) =1|X|​∑x′∈X𝒞⁡(a​x′)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|X|}\sum_{x^{\prime}\in X}\mathcal{C}(ax^{\prime})

where C:=1|X|​∑x′∈X¬B​Pc⁡(x′)C:=\frac{1}{|X|}\sum_{x^{\prime}\in X_{\neg BP}}c(x^{\prime}) is independent of aa. Corollary A.18.

Let A⊂𝒳A\subset\mathcal{X} be a finite set of candidates with 2≤|A|<∞2\leq|A|<\infty, and let X⊂𝒳X\subset\mathcal{X} be a finite set of strings with |X|>0|X|>0. Let Zp:=∑x′∈ℬ​𝒫​(p)Nq,x​(x′)Z_{p}:=\sum_{x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{BP}(p)}N_{q,x}(x^{\prime}) be the mass of ℬ​𝒫​(p)\mathcal{BP}(p) under Nq,xN_{q,x}. With i.i.d. sampling X∼Nq,x⊗kX\sim N_{q,x}^{\otimes k},

Pr⁡(XB​P=∅)=(1−Zp)k,\Pr(X_{BP}=\emptyset)=(1-Z_{p})^{k},

so with probability (1−Zp)k(1-Z_{p})^{k} selection produces no mean-fitness gain and the update reduces to the mutation term in (7). Under BP sampling, XB​P=XX_{BP}=X always, avoiding these zero-signal generations.

Lemma A.19 (Reusing the same evaluation set reduces variance of pairwise gaps).

Fix any distribution μ\mu over noisy inputs. Let XX and YY be independent sets with |X|=|Y|=k|X|=|Y|=k, where elements are drawn i.i.d. from μ\mu. Recall

f^​(a,X):=1k​∑x′∈X𝒞⁡(a​x′).\hat{f}(a,X):=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{x^{\prime}\in X}\mathcal{C}(ax^{\prime}).

For two candidates a,a′a,a^{\prime}, define the shared-set and independent-set gap estimators

Δ^shared:=f^​(a,X)−f^​(a′,X),Δ^ind:=f^​(a,X)−f^​(a′,Y).\widehat{\Delta}^{\mathrm{shared}}:=\hat{f}(a,X)-\hat{f}(a^{\prime},X),\qquad\widehat{\Delta}^{\mathrm{ind}}:=\hat{f}(a,X)-\hat{f}(a^{\prime},Y).

Both are unbiased estimators of 𝔼x′∼μ​[𝒞⁡(a​x′)−𝒞⁡(a′​x′)]\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}\sim\mu}[\mathcal{C}(ax^{\prime})-\mathcal{C}(a^{\prime}x^{\prime})], and

𝕍⁡(Δ^ind)−𝕍⁡(Δ^shared)=2k​Covx′∼μ​(𝒞⁡(a​x′),𝒞⁡(a′​x′)).\mathbb{V}(\widehat{\Delta}^{\mathrm{ind}})-\mathbb{V}(\widehat{\Delta}^{\mathrm{shared}})=\frac{2}{k}\,\mathrm{Cov}_{x^{\prime}\sim\mu}\!\big(\mathcal{C}(ax^{\prime}),\mathcal{C}(a^{\prime}x^{\prime})\big). (26)

In particular, if Cov⁡(𝒞⁡(a​x′),𝒞⁡(a′​x′))≥0\mathrm{Cov}(\mathcal{C}(ax^{\prime}),\mathcal{C}(a^{\prime}x^{\prime}))\geq 0, then reusing the same evaluation set XX yields a lower-variance estimate of the pairwise fitness gap.

Proof.

Unbiasedness is immediate by linearity of expectation and i.i.d. sampling. For the variance gap, note that

𝕍⁡(Δ^shared)\displaystyle\mathbb{V}(\widehat{\Delta}^{\mathrm{shared}}) =1k​𝕍​(𝒞⁡(a​x′)−𝒞⁡(a′​x′))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{k}\mathbb{V}\big(\mathcal{C}(ax^{\prime})-\mathcal{C}(a^{\prime}x^{\prime})\big)
𝕍⁡(Δ^ind)\displaystyle\mathbb{V}(\widehat{\Delta}^{\mathrm{ind}}) =1k​𝕍​(𝒞⁡(a​x′))+1k​𝕍​(𝒞⁡(a′​x′)),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{k}\mathbb{V}(\mathcal{C}(ax^{\prime}))+\frac{1}{k}\mathbb{V}(\mathcal{C}(a^{\prime}x^{\prime})),

(using i.i.d. averaging and independence between XX and YY). Finally,

𝕍⁡(𝒞⁡(a​x′)−𝒞⁡(a′​x′))\displaystyle\mathbb{V}\big(\mathcal{C}(ax^{\prime})-\mathcal{C}(a^{\prime}x^{\prime})\big)
=𝕍⁡(𝒞⁡(a​x′))+𝕍⁡(𝒞⁡(a′​x′))−2​C​o​v​(𝒞⁡(a​x′),𝒞⁡(a′​x′)),\displaystyle=\mathbb{V}(\mathcal{C}(ax^{\prime}))+\mathbb{V}(\mathcal{C}(a^{\prime}x^{\prime}))-2\mathrm{Cov}(\mathcal{C}(ax^{\prime}),\mathcal{C}(a^{\prime}x^{\prime})),

which yields (26). ∎

Remark A.20 (Why a positive covariance is plausible in BPJ).

The covariance term in (26) is often expected to be nonnegative even when aa and a′a^{\prime} are not in edit distance. A useful mental model is that each noisy input x′x^{\prime} carries a latent difficulty variable D=D⁡(x′)D=D(x^{\prime}) (or a small number of latent factors) that captures how close x′x^{\prime} is to the monitor’s decision boundary. Conditional on DD, different prefixes aa induce different pass probabilities, but these probabilities typically co-move with difficulty: for most aa, the function D↦Pr⁡(𝒞⁡(a​x′)=1∣D)D\mapsto\Pr(\mathcal{C}(ax^{\prime})=1\mid D) increases in “easiness” (encoded by DD) increases.

Inputs that are globally “easy” tend to make many prefixes pass, while globally “hard” inputs tend to make many prefixes fail. This positive correlation is exactly what makes reusing the same evaluation set reduce the variance of pairwise comparisons (Lemma A.19).

A.7 Theory limitations

This appendix section provides a stylised dynamical-systems view of BPJ. The results are intended to be diagnostic (to clarify what factors can drive progress and when continuation can fail), not to furnish end-to-end guarantees of success. Key limitations are as follows.

Mean-field or infinite-population approximation.

We analyse the infinite-population limit pt∈Δ⁡(𝒳)p_{t}\in\Delta(\mathcal{X}), whereas BPJ runs with a finite population and strong elitism. Finite-population effects introduce genetic drift, premature loss of pmf support, and additional stochasticity in quantile estimates. As a result, statements about equilibria, covariance driven progress, and local stability should be interpreted as describing an idealised expectation behaviour.

Deterministic fitness vs. stochastic evaluation.

Most of the dynamical analysis assumes access to the exact relaxed fitness fq​(a)=𝔼x′∼Nq,x​[𝒞⁡(a​x′)]f_{q}(a)=\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}\sim N_{q,x}}[\mathcal{C}(ax^{\prime})]. In practice, BPJ uses a finite evaluation set and obtains f^q​(a)\hat{f}_{q}(a), yielding a stochastic update. This creates (i) noise in rankings/top-α\alpha membership, (ii) potential bias when using adaptive sampling (e.g. boundary-point sampling), and (iii) additional correlations across candidates when a shared evaluation set is reused.

Hard vs. soft quantile selection mismatch.

Convergence and continuation arguments are stated for the soft selection operator (so that Φqsoft\Phi_{q}^{\mathrm{soft}} is smooth and implicit-function tools apply), whereas BPJ uses hard top-KK selection (discontinuous truncation) and finite populations. Hard truncation can create zeros in the support and discontinuous changes in the selected set when the quantile cutoff crosses ties, making global stability and continuation more delicate. Thus, the soft-quantile analysis should be read as a surrogate that captures qualitative phenomena (e.g. local attractors, bifurcation/ill-conditioning) but not as a exact model of BPJ dynamics.

Local (not global) results: branch switching and bifurcations.

The continuation statement is local: it guarantees trackability only when (I−Dp​Φqsoft)(I-D_{p}\Phi_{q}^{\mathrm{soft}}) remains invertible and the equilibrium remains locally attracting. When that condition is violated, there can be abrupt changes in equilibria and changes in basin of attraction. Empirically, such events can manifest as plateaus or sudden jumps in the curriculum schedule. Our current theory does not characterise their probability or impact. Such characterisation would require assumptions on the global structure of fitness landscape.

Mutation operator idealisation.

Mutation is modelled as a time-homogeneous Markov kernel M(⋅∣a)M(\cdot\mid a) on 𝒳\mathcal{X}. BPJ’s actual edit operations may depend on candidate length, tokenisation, constraints, and heuristics. Moreover, if MM is not sufficiently mixing (typical for local edits), global contraction is unlikely and the dynamics may be highly sensitive to initialisation and to the particular selection rule.

Alignment conditions are descriptive, not guaranteed.

The alignment factor Γtq\Gamma_{t}^{q} formalises when selection under fqf_{q} increases mass on the base success set A1A^{1}. However, the theory does not provide conditions under which Γtq>0\Gamma_{t}^{q}>0 holds for a given monitor/classifier or perturbation process. In particular, relaxed objectives can admit spurious high-fitness regions that do not correspond to A1A^{1}. Hence the alignment discussion explains what must be true for continuation to help, but does not prove it is true in general.

Boundary-point (BP) sampling: partial formalisation.

The BP sampling discussion establishes rank-preservation only under specific conditions (e.g. hard quantile selection and a fixed reference population for defining ℬ​𝒫​(⋅)\mathcal{BP}(\cdot)). In BPJ, the BP set drifts over optimisation iterations, and the sampling distribution is adaptive. A complete theory would need to (i) specify the maintenance protocol, (ii) handle cases where the boundary set is empty or extremely low-mass (Zp≈0Z_{p}\approx 0), and (iii) quantify the query complexity and ranking error under adaptive, non-i.i.d. sampling.

Appendix D Additional Plots

We provide additional results referenced in the paper. More detailed results focus mostly on prompted GPT4.1-nano classifier setting as we decided to not share detailed insights on vulnerabilities in currently deployed safeguards.

Appendix E Single-Interaction Defences

Upon replicating our attack, Anthropic has conducted preliminary analysis and found:

  • •

    Probe-based classifiers (Cunningham et al., 2026) may be more resistant to this type of attack than text-based classifier, potentially due to adversarial prefixes being more difficult to find for probe-based defences.

  • •

    Training classifiers on effective BPJ attack strings may improve detection of unseen BPJ strings.

  • •

    Randomly serving one of two similarly trained classifiers may improve robustness, despite each classifier being individually vulnerable.
